The search turned up no Booker Prize winners from 1950, because the prize did not exist then. It was first awarded in 1969. When it began in 1969, the goal of the Booker Prize was to increase readership of quality fiction, and the first award went to P.H. Newby's novel Something to Answer For.

Books from 1950 were not eligible in any case. In 1969 and 1970 the prize was awarded to a novel published in the year previous to that in which the prize was given. That means the 1969 prize covered 1968 novels, and the 1970 prize covered 1969 novels. Under the later rule, from 1971 onwards, it was awarded to books published in the same year as the prize.

One related result: Newby did publish a 1950 novel, The Young May Moon (1950), but that book was not a Booker entry. The search did not surface any other 1950 publications by Booker winners.

The search confirms that *The Young May Moon* is a 1950 P.H. Newby novel, first published in London, with a US edition following in 1951.

- **UK first edition (1950):** Jonathan Cape published it in London in 1950, according to [bookseller listings](https://biblio.co.uk/book/young-may-moon-newby-ph/d/652056405). The [phnewby.net bibliography](https://phnewby.net/books/) also lists it as a 1950 novel.
- **Contemporary reviews:** The [Spectator's February 1950 issue](https://archive.spectator.co.uk/article/3rd-february-1950/28/fiction) reviewed it and found it disappointing, and a [March 1950 Spectator listing](https://archive.spectator.co.uk/article/24th-march-1950/19/-switzerland-12s-6d) included it among recent novels.
- **US edition (1951):** One [bookseller record](https://biblio.co.uk/book/young-may-moon-newby-ph/d/1565724116) gives the publisher as Alfred A. Knopf, New York, dated 1951. A [Time review](https://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,814276,00.html) also names Knopf as publisher, priced at $3, but the search result gives no date.
- **Other reference:** Anthony West reviewed the novel in *The New Yorker* on January 27, 1951, as cited in the [phnewby.net bibliography](https://phnewby.net/resources/).

Some of these sources are bookseller listings and secondary bibliographic pages, so the exact dates are best confirmed against a library catalogue.

Gwendolyn Brooks was born in Topeka, Kansas, and her best-known 1950 achievement was the Pulitzer Prize for *Annie Allen*, not a new 1950 book.

- **Birthplace:** Brooks was born in Topeka on June 7, 1917. At the age of five weeks, she and her mother returned to the Brooks's residence in Chicago, the city in which Brooks would live for most of her life.
- **The 1950 award:** Sources disagree on the date of the award. Wikipedia gives May 1, 1950, for Annie Allen, making her the first African American to receive a Pulitzer Prize. A BET piece dates it to Sept. 27, 1950.
- **Publication date of *Annie Allen*:** One source says Annie Allen, published in 1949, while another says it was published in 1950. The book is usually described as her second poetry collection.
- **Other 1950 work:** Brooks wrote the essay "Poets Who Are Negroes" (1950).
- **Nearby titles:** Her first collection was A Street in Bronzeville (1945). Her prose novella Maud Martha (1953) came later.

P.H. Newby (Percy Howard Newby) was born in Crowborough, Sussex, England, on 25 June 1918. One source specifies East Sussex, which is the modern county. Percy Howard Newby was born June 25, 1918, in Crowborough, East Sussex, England. He was also known as Howard Newby. He was educated at Hanley Castle Grammar School in Worcestershire, and St Paul's College of Education in Cheltenham.

Annie Allen was published in 1949 and won the 1950 Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.

- **Publication (1949):** Harper & Brothers issued the book in 1949. The Chicago Literary Archive gives August 24, 1949 as the date, while Wikipedia lists October 1, 1949. Both dates are in 1949. (Annie Allen (1949) was Gwendolyn Brooks's second poetry collection.) The University of Illinois exhibit and the Columbia Pulitzer collection record also list 1949.
- **Pulitzer (1950):** The prize went to the book in 1950, making Brooks the first African American Pulitzer winner in any category. The Pulitzer's own article describes the 1950 jury's process, which included the book as an entry.
- **Outlier:** SuperSummary lists a 1972 publication year and Greenwood Press as publisher. That conflicts with every other source here and looks like a reprint or catalog error, so I would not rely on it.

Overall, the search supports 1949 as the original publication year and 1950 as the Pulitzer year.
